q: Who was Moses' father-in-law, described as the priest of Midian?
explain: Jethro (also called Reuel) was priest of Midian; he later advised Moses to appoint judges to share the work.

q: Which woman was judging Israel while sitting under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel?
explain: Deborah, a prophet, judged Israel and summoned Barak against Sisera. Jael killed Sisera, but she was not a judge.

q: Who was the mother of the prophet Samuel?
explain: Hannah prayed for a son at Shiloh and dedicated Samuel to the LORD. Peninnah was her husband's other wife.

q: Ruth the Moabite was the great-grandmother of which king?
explain: Ruth and Boaz had Obed, Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.

q: Who resolved to approach the king uninvited, saying "if I perish, I perish"?
explain: Esther agreed to go to King Ahasuerus without being summoned, which could mean death, after asking the Jews of Susa to fast for her.

q: Which prisoner did Pilate release at the crowd's demand instead of Jesus?
explain: Pilate customarily released a prisoner at the feast; the crowd chose Barabbas. Simon of Cyrene carried Jesus' cross; Malchus was the high priest's servant whose ear was cut off.

q: Which chief tax collector climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus?
explain: Zacchaeus of Jericho was short, so he climbed a sycamore; Jesus invited himself to his house.

q: Who is the first follower of Jesus whose martyrdom Acts records?
explain: Stephen was stoned after his speech to the council (Acts 7). James son of Zebedee was killed later by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12).

q: Peter raised which disciple, known for good works and charity, from the dead in Joppa?
explain: Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, was raised in Joppa. Aeneas was a paralysed man Peter healed in Lydda; Eutychus was revived by Paul in Troas.

q: Which young man fell asleep and fell from a third-storey window during Paul's long talk at Troas?
explain: Eutychus fell and was taken up dead, but Paul embraced him and said his life was in him.

q: Who was Jacob's firstborn son?
explain: Leah bore Reuben first. He later lost the privileges of the firstborn because he slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine.

q: Which of Abraham's relatives chose the Jordan plain and settled near Sodom?
explain: When their herds became too large, Lot chose the well-watered Jordan valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom.

q: Which disciple of Jesus is also called Didymus, meaning "Twin"?
explain: John's Gospel three times calls Thomas "Didymus."

q: Who was the king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abram?
explain: Melchizedek brought bread and wine and blessed Abram, who gave him a tenth. Hebrews links Jesus' priesthood to his.

q: Who took Apollos aside in Ephesus and explained the way of God to him more accurately?
explain: Apollos knew only the baptism of John; Priscilla and Aquila taught him more fully.

q: In which village did Jesus perform his first sign, turning water into wine?
explain: John calls the wedding miracle at Cana in Galilee the first of Jesus' signs.

q: Where did Elijah challenge the prophets of Baal to a contest of sacrifice?
explain: The contest took place on Mount Carmel; fire fell on Elijah's sacrifice.

q: Where did King Saul and his son Jonathan die in battle with the Philistines?
explain: Saul's sons were killed and Saul fell on his own sword on Mount Gilboa.

q: In which city were the disciples first called "Christians"?
explain: Barnabas and Saul taught at Antioch for a year, and there the disciples were first called Christians.

q: In which city did Paul speak at the Areopagus about an altar "to an unknown god"?
explain: Paul addressed the Areopagus in Athens, starting from an altar inscription.

q: Near which city did Jesus ask "Who do you say that I am?" and Peter confess him as the Christ (in Matthew and Mark)?
explain: Matthew and Mark place the confession in the district of Caesarea Philippi, near the sources of the Jordan.

q: On which island was John when he received the visions of Revelation?
explain: John says he was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.

q: On which island was Paul shipwrecked on his way to Rome?
explain: After two weeks adrift the ship ran aground on Malta, where Paul survived a viper bite and healed Publius' father.

q: Abram's family set out for Canaan from which city of the Chaldeans?
explain: Terah took Abram, Sarai and Lot from Ur of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran on the way to Canaan.

q: Jonah boarded a ship at Joppa to flee to which destination?
explain: Jonah went the opposite way from Nineveh, heading for Tarshish, usually located in the far west Mediterranean.

q: Where did Jacob dream of a stairway reaching to heaven?
explain: Jacob named the place Bethel, "house of God." Peniel is where he later wrestled with God.

q: In which town did Jesus raise a widow's only son during his funeral procession?
explain: Only Luke records the raising of the widow's son at the gate of Nain. Lazarus was raised at Bethany.

q: Which Old Testament book never explicitly names God in its Hebrew text?
explain: Esther never names God, though many see his providence in its events, as in Mordecai's "relief and deliverance will rise from another place."

q: Which is the longest psalm, an extended acrostic meditation on God's word?
explain: Psalm 119 has 176 verses: 22 stanzas of 8 lines, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

q: Which New Testament letter is addressed to a believer about his slave Onesimus?
explain: Paul appeals to Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother."

q: Which Gospel opens with "In the beginning was the Word"?
explain: John's prologue echoes Genesis 1:1 and identifies the Word who became flesh.

q: Which New Testament books are both addressed to Theophilus?
explain: Both open by addressing Theophilus, and Acts refers back to "the first book."

q: Which book is a series of mostly acrostic poems mourning the destruction of Jerusalem?
explain: Chapters 1-4 of Lamentations are alphabetic acrostics; chapter 5 has 22 lines but is not an acrostic.

q: Which is the shortest book of the Old Testament by number of verses?
explain: Obadiah has 21 verses in one chapter.

q: Which book contains the chapter often called the "hall of faith," listing Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and others?
explain: Hebrews 11 recounts what the faithful did "by faith."

q: Which prophetic book contains the vision of a valley of dry bones coming to life?
explain: Ezekiel 37 pictures Israel's national restoration as bones receiving flesh and breath.

q: Which chapter of 1 Corinthians is the famous description of love that is patient and kind?
explain: Chapter 13 sits between Paul's discussions of spiritual gifts in chapters 12 and 14.

q: Which letter argues that "faith apart from works is dead"?
explain: James insists genuine faith shows itself in action, using Abraham and Rahab as examples.

q: In the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), which book comes last?
explain: The Tanakh ends with Chronicles, closing on Cyrus' decree to rebuild the temple. Christian Old Testaments, following the Greek order, end with Malachi.

q: Around when did the northern kingdom of Israel fall to Assyria?
explain: Samaria fell after a three-year siege, conventionally dated 722 (or 721) BC.

q: Around when did Babylon destroy Jerusalem and Solomon's temple?
explain: Most date the fall to 586 BC, though some argue for 587 BC.

q: Around when did the united kingdom split into Israel and Judah after Solomon?
explain: The division followed Solomon's death and Rehoboam's harsh answer to the northern tribes; common chronologies place it about 931/930 BC.

q: In what year did Cyrus of Persia capture Babylon, opening the way for exiles to return?
explain: Babylon fell to the Persians in 539 BC; Cyrus' decree followed in his first year over Babylon.

q: When was the second temple completed?
options: About 516/515 BC, in the sixth year of Darius
explain: Ezra says it was finished in the sixth year of Darius I. Herod later expanded it massively from about 20 BC.

q: Which of these happened first?
explain: Whether dated early (about 1446 BC) or late (about 1260 BC), the exodus precedes the monarchy, the exile and the return.

q: In what year did the Romans destroy the Jerusalem temple, as Jesus had foretold?
explain: Roman forces under Titus destroyed the temple in AD 70. Jesus had said not one stone would be left on another.

q: Herod the Great is usually thought to have died about 4 BC. What does that imply about Jesus' birth?
options: It probably happened a few years before AD 1
It came several years after Herod's death
It must have been after AD 6
explain: Matthew places Jesus' birth during Herod's reign. The AD system was calculated centuries later and is slightly off; a minority dates Herod's death to 1 BC.

q: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I. About when was that?
explain: The twentieth year of Artaxerxes I falls around 445/444 BC.

q: Which of these prophets ministered earliest?
explain: Elijah was active in the 9th century BC under Ahab; Isaiah in the 8th, Jeremiah in the 7th-6th, Malachi in the 5th.

q: Which prophet was among the herdsmen of Tekoa?
explain: Amos, from Tekoa in Judah, was sent to prophesy to the northern kingdom.

q: Which prophet was told to marry Gomer as a sign of Israel's unfaithfulness?
explain: Hosea's marriage to Gomer pictured God's relationship with unfaithful Israel.

q: Who saw the Lord high and lifted up "in the year that King Uzziah died"?
explain: Isaiah's temple vision includes the seraphim crying "Holy, holy, holy" and his commission.

q: Which prophet was commanded not to take a wife or have children, as a sign of coming disaster?
explain: Jeremiah's celibacy signalled that families in Judah would perish.

q: Which prophet was told not to mourn openly when his wife died, as a sign to the exiles?
explain: God called Ezekiel's wife "the delight of your eyes"; his restrained grief prefigured the people's reaction to the temple's fall.

q: Who asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit?
explain: Elisha asked for the firstborn's share of Elijah's spirit and took up his mantle.

q: Which prophetic book is entirely an oracle against Edom?
explain: Obadiah condemns Edom for gloating over Jerusalem's fall. Nahum is directed against Nineveh.

q: Which prophet foretold that a ruler would come from Bethlehem Ephrathah?
explain: The chief priests cite Micah to Herod when the magi ask where the Messiah is to be born.

q: Which prophet's promise of the Spirit poured out on all flesh does Peter quote at Pentecost?
explain: Peter says the Pentecost events are "what was uttered through the prophet Joel."

q: Which prophetess did King Josiah's officials consult about the newly found Book of the Law?
explain: Huldah confirmed the book's warnings but promised Josiah would die before the disaster. Noadiah opposed Nehemiah; Anna appears in Luke.

q: Who was the first king of Israel?
explain: Samuel anointed Saul of the tribe of Benjamin as the first king.

q: Which queen seized the throne of Judah and tried to destroy the royal family?
explain: Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, ruled about six years until the hidden boy Joash was crowned.

q: Which king led a sweeping reform after the Book of the Law was found in the temple?
explain: Josiah tore his clothes on hearing the book read and renewed the covenant.

q: Which king set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan?
explain: Jeroboam feared his people would return to Jerusalem to worship, so he built rival shrines.

q: Which king of Judah was struck with a skin disease for burning incense in the temple?
explain: Uzziah grew proud and usurped a priestly duty; he lived in isolation until he died.

q: Which king spread Sennacherib's threatening letter before the LORD and saw Jerusalem delivered?
explain: Hezekiah prayed in the temple; Isaiah brought God's answer, and the Assyrian army was struck down.

q: Which king of Judah reigned 55 years and, according to Chronicles, repented in captivity?
explain: Kings records Manasseh's long and wicked reign; Chronicles adds his humbling in Babylon and restoration.

q: Which army commander was anointed king of Israel at Elisha's instruction and destroyed Ahab's dynasty?
explain: A young prophet sent by Elisha anointed Jehu at Ramoth-gilead.

q: Which foreign king does Isaiah call the LORD's "anointed"?
explain: Isaiah names Cyrus as the one God would use to rebuild Jerusalem and free the exiles.

q: What was the result of Rehoboam's harsh reply to the northern tribes?
options: The northern tribes rejected him and made Jeroboam king
explain: Following younger advisers, Rehoboam threatened heavier burdens; ten tribes broke away.

q: Who was chosen by lot to replace Judas among the Twelve?
explain: Two candidates were put forward; the lot fell on Matthias.

q: Which of the Twelve is the first whose death Acts records?
explain: Herod Agrippa I killed James with the sword. Stephen died earlier but was not one of the Twelve.

q: Which brothers did Jesus nickname "Boanerges," sons of thunder?
explain: Mark records the nickname in the list of the Twelve.

q: In John's Gospel, who first brought his brother Simon to Jesus?
explain: Andrew told Simon, "We have found the Messiah," and brought him to Jesus.

q: Who told Nathanael about Jesus and answered his doubts with "Come and see"?
explain: Nathanael asked whether anything good could come from Nazareth; Philip replied, "Come and see."

q: In Galatians, Paul says Peter was entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised and he with the gospel to whom?
explain: James, Cephas and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship for the Gentile mission.

q: Which of the Twelve was a tax collector when Jesus called him?
explain: Matthew's Gospel calls him "Matthew the tax collector"; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

q: Who does Paul greet with Andronicus as "of note among the apostles," a phrase whose meaning is debated?
explain: Interpreters debate whether the phrase means prominent as apostles or well known to the apostles, and earlier some read the name as a male "Junias."

q: Church tradition most commonly identifies the anonymous "disciple whom Jesus loved" as which apostle?
explain: The Gospel never names him. Second-century tradition identifies him with John; some modern scholars propose other candidates.

q: Who was the man the apostles called Barnabas, "son of encouragement"?
explain: Barnabas sold a field and gave the money to the apostles. John Mark was his cousin.

q: The Council of Nicaea (AD 325) was called chiefly to address which controversy?
options: Pelagianism, about grace and free will
Arianism, whether the Son is fully divine
explain: Nicaea affirmed that the Son is "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father against Arius. It also dealt with the date of Easter and other matters.

q: Which emperor, together with Licinius, agreed in 313 to grant Christians legal toleration (the "Edict of Milan")?
explain: Constantine and Licinius agreed on religious toleration in 313. Diocletian had led the Great Persecution; Theodosius later made Nicene Christianity the state religion.

q: In which town did Martin Luther publish his Ninety-five Theses in 1517?
explain: Luther was a professor at Wittenberg. Geneva was Calvin's city, Zurich Zwingli's, and Worms the site of the 1521 diet.

q: Augustine served as bishop of which North African city?
explain: Augustine was converted in Milan, influenced by Ambrose, and became bishop of Hippo Regius. His *Confessions* describes reading Romans 13 at his conversion.

q: Irenaeus of Lyon wrote *Against Heresies* chiefly to refute which teaching?
explain: Irenaeus (late 2nd century) opposed Gnostic systems such as Valentinianism, appealing to apostolic tradition and the goodness of creation. The other movements arose later.

q: What did the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) define about Christ?
options: One person in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation
One nature, the divine absorbing the human
Two persons joined by moral union
A man adopted as Son at his baptism
explain: Chalcedon's definition became the standard for Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches; the Oriental Orthodox churches did not accept it.

q: What is the central claim of Peter's Pentecost sermon?
options: The temple must be rebuilt for the Messiah
Jesus was a prophet who will return as Elijah
Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved
God raised the crucified Jesus and made him Lord and Christ
explain: Peter argues from Joel and the Psalms that the risen and exalted Jesus has poured out the Spirit.

q: Who produced the Latin translation of the Bible later known as the Vulgate?
explain: Jerome worked in the late 4th and early 5th centuries, translating much of the Old Testament directly from Hebrew.

q: The split between Eastern and Western churches is conventionally dated to which year?
explain: Mutual excommunications in 1054 symbolise a separation that developed over centuries.

q: Who produced the first printed English New Testament translated from the Greek?
explain: Tyndale's New Testament was printed in 1526; he was executed in 1536. Wycliffite Bibles were earlier but handwritten and translated from Latin.

q: What does amillennialism hold about the thousand years of Revelation 20?
options: They symbolise Christ's present reign between his first and second comings
Christ returns before a future thousand-year reign on earth
Christ returns after the gospel brings an extended era of flourishing
The thousand years were fulfilled entirely in AD 70
explain: Amillennialists read Revelation 20 as describing the current age, with Satan bound so the gospel can go to the nations.

q: What does premillennialism hold?
options: Christ will return before a future reign on earth, the millennium
The millennium is the present church age
Christ returns after a golden age of gospel success
There will be no future resurrection of the body
explain: Premillennialists, historic and dispensational, read Revelation 20 as following Christ's return in Revelation 19.

q: What does postmillennialism hold?
options: Christ returns after an extended era in which the gospel transforms much of the world
Christ returns before a literal thousand-year reign
The world will steadily worsen until a secret rapture
explain: Postmillennialists draw on the growth parables and the Great Commission to expect widespread gospel success before Christ comes.

q: What does the penal substitution view of the atonement hold?
options: Christ's death chiefly defeats the powers of sin, death and the devil
Christ's death chiefly reveals God's love to move us to repentance
Christ bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners
Christ's death restored God's offended honour by satisfaction
explain: Defenders appeal to texts on the servant bearing iniquity and Christ made sin for us. The distractors summarise Christus Victor, moral influence and Anselm's satisfaction view.

q: What does the Christus Victor view of the atonement emphasise?
options: Christ's death and resurrection defeat sin, death and the devil
Christ pays a legal penalty owed to divine justice
Christ restores God's honour as a feudal lord
explain: Associated with early church writers and revived by Gustaf Aulen, it highlights Christ triumphing over the powers.

q: What does conditional immortality (annihilationism) hold about the final state of the lost?
options: All will eventually be reconciled to God
They are ultimately destroyed and cease to exist
They are reincarnated for another chance
explain: Proponents argue immortality is God's gift to the redeemed and read "destroy" and "perish" literally.

q: What does the credobaptist view hold?
options: The infant children of believers should be baptised
Baptism is for those who personally profess faith in Christ
Baptism is unnecessary because it is purely inward
Only those baptised by an apostle are truly baptised
explain: Credobaptists point to the pattern of belief then baptism in Acts.

q: What does the paedobaptist view hold?
options: Only adults who profess faith may be baptised
Children of believers should be baptised as members of the covenant community
Baptism should be delayed until death
explain: Paedobaptists point to household baptisms and the link between circumcision and baptism, though traditions differ on what baptism effects.

q: What does complementarianism hold about men and women?
options: They are equal in dignity but have some distinct roles, with certain church and home leadership reserved for men
All roles in church and home are open to both on the basis of gifting
Women are less in the image of God than men
Women may not take any part in church ministry
explain: Complementarians affirm equal worth (Gen 1:27) and cite passages on elders and household order. The last two options are straw men that complementarians reject.

q: What does egalitarianism hold about men and women in ministry?
options: Certain leadership roles are reserved for qualified men
Men and women are identical with no differences
All ministries and leadership roles are open to women and men on the basis of gifting and calling
Leadership belongs only to unmarried believers
explain: Egalitarians point to women prophets, co-workers and mutual submission. The claim that they deny all differences between the sexes is a straw man.

q: What does cessationism hold about spiritual gifts?
options: All gifts continue unchanged until Christ returns
Certain miraculous and revelatory gifts ceased after the apostolic era
No spiritual gifts were ever miraculous
Gifts are given only to ordained clergy
explain: Cessationists argue sign gifts authenticated the apostles and the foundational revelation. Continuationists read "when the perfect comes" as Christ's return.

q: Why was the Samaritan woman surprised that Jesus asked her for a drink?
options: Jews and Samaritans generally avoided dealings with each other
explain: John explains that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans; the hostility had roots in rival temples and histories.

q: In Jesus' parable of the vineyard labourers, a denarius represents what?
options: A typical day's wage for a labourer
explain: The owner agrees with workers for a denarius a day.

q: What did the feast of Passover commemorate?
options: The giving of the law at Sinai
God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt
explain: Passover remembers the night the LORD passed over Israel's houses and struck Egypt's firstborn. Purim celebrates the victory over Haman.

q: Why did Israelites live in temporary shelters during the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles)?
options: To mourn the destruction of the temple
To prepare for the barley harvest
To remember that God made Israel live in booths after the exodus
To honour the patriarchs' tents in Canaan
explain: Leviticus explains the booths as a reminder of the wilderness journey.

q: Which group denied the resurrection of the dead?
explain: Acts says the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, angel or spirit, while the Pharisees acknowledge them.

q: What was the Sanhedrin?
options: The chief Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest
explain: Jesus, Peter and John, Stephen and Paul all appeared before the council.

q: The Jewish feast of Pentecost, when the Spirit came in Acts 2, is also known as what?
options: The Feast of Weeks, fifty days after the Passover-season offering
explain: The feast was counted as seven weeks plus one day, giving the Greek name "fiftieth."

q: On the Day of Atonement, what did the high priest alone do?
options: Read the whole law to the people
Enter the Most Holy Place with blood once a year
Offer the first sheaf of barley
explain: Leviticus 16 prescribes the ritual; Hebrews contrasts it with Christ entering once for all.

q: In what languages was the notice "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" written on the cross, according to John?
explain: John says it was written in Hebrew (likely Aramaic), Latin and Greek, so passers-by could read it.

q: What was the purpose of levirate marriage in Israel?
options: To provide a second wife for a priest
For a brother to marry his dead brother's childless widow and raise up a name for him
explain: Deuteronomy describes the custom; Boaz acts in a related role as kinsman-redeemer for Ruth.

q: What trade did Paul share with Aquila and Priscilla?
explain: Paul stayed and worked with them in Corinth because they were tentmakers by trade.

q: Mark calls Jesus a *tektōn*. What does the Greek word most likely mean?
options: A craftsman or builder working mainly in wood or stone
A scribe trained in the law
A fisherman owning his own boat
explain: Traditionally translated "carpenter," the word covers builders and craftsmen more broadly.

q: What did Lydia of Thyatira trade in?
explain: Luke calls her a seller of purple goods; Thyatira was known for dyeing.

q: Peter stayed in Joppa with a man named Simon who practised which trade?
explain: Peter lodged with Simon the tanner, whose house was by the sea, and had his rooftop vision there.

q: What position did Nehemiah hold at the Persian court?
explain: Nehemiah's closeness to Artaxerxes let him request leave to rebuild Jerusalem.

q: How does Paul describe Luke in Colossians?
explain: Paul sends greetings from "Luke the beloved physician."

q: How did Amos describe his work before God called him?
options: A herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs
A trained son of the prophets
explain: Amos denies being a professional prophet; the LORD took him from following the flock.

q: Which son of Isaac was "a skilful hunter, a man of the field"?
explain: Esau hunted while Jacob was a quiet man who stayed among the tents; Isaac loved Esau's game.

q: Jeremiah went down to the house of which craftsman to receive a message about God's sovereignty over nations?
explain: Watching a potter rework a spoiled vessel, Jeremiah heard that God could do the same with Israel.

q: What were Simon Peter and Andrew doing when Jesus called them to follow him in Mark?
options: Casting a net into the Sea of Galilee
explain: They were fishermen; Jesus said he would make them fishers of people.
